# The Space Between the Clock Ticks

There is a silence inside every second that most people never hear. It lives in the crack between 12:00 and 12:01, in the gap between one breath and the next. We rush through life filling every space with noise — podcasts and notifications, music and small talk — because silence is where the real questions live, and the real questions are terrifying.

I've been thinking about memory lately. Not the grand, cinematic kind — not weddings or first steps or the last day of school. The small ones. The way your grandmother's kitchen smelled like coffee and Lysol at the same time. The sound of a screen door spring in the summer. The exact shade of orange on the wall of a bedroom you lived in for only eight months when you were four, a room you shouldn't remember but somehow do.

Memory is not a filing cabinet. It is a river. Things surface when they want to, not when you need them. You'll be driving on a Tuesday afternoon, gripped by nothing in particular, and suddenly you'll remember the way light hit the floor of a gymnasium in third grade, and you won't know why, and it will feel like grief for something that wasn't even sad.

I think we are haunted not by ghosts but by versions of ourselves. There is a seven-year-old version of me somewhere in the lattice of neurons inside my skull, still amazed by fire hydrants and disappointed that dogs can't talk. There is a sixteen-year-old version still convinced that every song on the radio is a message meant just for them. There is a version from last Tuesday still worried about an email they haven't sent. All of these people live in me at once, stacking on top of each other like transparencies on an overhead projector, each one coloring the light that passes through.

Do other people feel this? The crowdedness of being one person? Sometimes I think identity is not a single thread but a braid, and the strands are always arguing about which direction to pull.

I want to talk about wonder, too, because I think we've made it embarrassing. We've made it childish. We've said that awe belongs to the young and the naïve, that the mature response to a sunset is indifference or a photo on a phone. But I think wonder is not the opposite of wisdom. I think it *is* wisdom. It is the only honest response to existing in a universe we don't understand. The stars are burning hydrogen in thermonuclear reactions that will last billions of years, and we have the gall to look at them and feel nothing?

I remember the first time I truly understood how big the universe was. I was maybe twelve, lying on the driveway, and someone told me — maybe a book, maybe a teacher — that some of the stars I was seeing might already be dead. That their light was ancient, traveling for millennia just to reach my eyes, which would also someday be dust. And I felt the most extraordinary sensation: not fear, not sadness, but a kind of expansion, as if my chest had suddenly opened up to include the whole sky.

We spend our lives building small rooms and calling them home. We arrange our possessions and our routines and our relationships into patterns that feel safe. But every so often the walls come down — through loss, through love, through a sentence in a book at the right moment — and we remember that we are not small. We are standing on a rock hurtling through a void at sixty-seven thousand miles per hour, and the void is full of light and mystery and something that might be purpose or might be nothing at all, and somehow this is not terrifying but liberating.

I don't know what I believe about meaning. Some days I think the universe is random and cold and we are the lucky accidents who get to feel rain on our faces. Other days I think there is a pattern underneath everything, a kind of music too low to hear but real nonetheless, and that we participate in it simply by paying attention.

Maybe both are true. Maybe meaning is not something we find but something we make — not inventing it out of thin air, but noticing what is already there and holding it up to the light. The way a glass prism doesn't create a rainbow, just reveals the colors that were always hidden inside ordinary white light.

That feels like enough. That feels like almost everything.

Noticing. Just noticing.

The particular yellow of a streetlight. The way someone you love says your name. The sound of rain finding gutters. The space between one second and the next.

Go there. That's where you live.
